what: Halozyme licenses a technology rather than selling a drug. Its enzyme lets biologic medicines be injected under the skin in minutes instead of infused for hours, and drugmakers pay royalties to use it.
customers: Large pharmaceutical companies that license the technology for their own drugs, principally Roche, Johnson & Johnson, Takeda and Argenx.
money: the largest and most profitable part
a share of partners' sales of drugs using the enzyme
the enzyme itself supplied to partners
moat: Patents on the enzyme and a decade of regulatory precedent: a partner that reformulates a blockbuster around it is committed for that drug's life.
risks: Royalty income depends on partners' sales, which Halozyme does not control
Key patents expire over the coming decade and competitors are developing alternative enzymes
$2.2B of debt against $134M of cash, from share buybacks
opportunities: A 22.7% net margin and $886M of free cash flow on $1.8B of revenue
Revenue grew from $443M to $1.4B in four years
Analysts see about 29% upside, and more partners keep converting infused drugs to injections
watch: Royalty revenue growth and any patent challenges to the core enzyme.
